course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

topic.title: Causation in Period 4
topic.summary: A guide to explaining the causes and effects of change from 1800 to 1848, and to judging the extent to which politics, economics, and foreign policy promoted an American identity.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is best described as a long-term cause of the rise of mass political parties?
choices: The expansion of suffrage and a market economy that created many wage earners
The nomination of Andrew Jackson as a presidential candidate in 1828
The defeat of John Quincy Adams in the presidential election of 1828
The decision of the Whigs to hold a national convention in 1839
questions.explanation: Long-term changes in who could vote and how Americans earned a living created the conditions for mass parties.
choiceExplanations: Long-term changes in who could vote and how Americans earned a living created the conditions for mass parties.
This was a short-term event, not a long-term cause.
An election result was a short-term effect.
The Whig convention was a result of party growth.
questions.distinguisher: The nomination choice is close because it affected parties directly, but it was a single event and not a long-term cause.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a short-term cause of the nullification crisis of 1832?
choices: The invention of the cotton gin in 1793
The signing of the Constitution in 1787
The passage of the tariffs of 1828 and 1832
The end of the Atlantic slave trade in 1808
questions.explanation: South Carolina acted in response to recent tariffs that it believed harmed its economy.
choiceExplanations: That was a very long-term influence on the Southern economy.
The Constitution was a long-term background factor.
South Carolina acted in response to recent tariffs that it believed harmed its economy.
That event came long before the tariff dispute.
questions.distinguisher: The cotton gin choice is close because the gin helped shape the Southern economy, but it was a long-term factor.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: How did the decisions of the Marshall Court promote a stronger national identity?
choices: They gave the states the final say on the meaning of the Constitution
They ended the power of Congress to regulate trade with other nations
They placed limits on the power of the federal courts to review state laws
They strengthened federal authority over the states
questions.explanation: McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden supported national supremacy and a national economy.
choiceExplanations: The decisions asserted national supremacy.
The Court upheld Congress's commerce power.
The Court asserted its power over state laws.
McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden supported national supremacy and a national economy.
questions.distinguisher: The states' final say choice is close because it describes a major dispute of the period, but the Marshall Court ruled for national authority.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: How did the War of 1812 contribute to a stronger American national identity?
choices: It gave the United States control of Canada and ended all disputes with Britain
Many Americans saw its end as a victory, and the Federalists lost influence
It divided the nation more deeply and led several New England states to leave the Union
It made Americans dependent on British manufactured goods for the next generation
questions.explanation: National pride grew after the war, and the Federalist Party, which had opposed it, lost influence.
choiceExplanations: The United States did not gain Canada.
National pride grew after the war, and the Federalist Party, which had opposed it, lost influence.
The Hartford Convention did not lead to secession.
The war encouraged American manufacturing.
questions.distinguisher: The Canada choice is close because some Americans had hoped to take Canada, but the treaty restored the prewar borders.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains how the market revolution both promoted and limited a shared national identity?
choices: It made every region produce the same goods and so ended all disputes over the tariff
It isolated each region from the others and ended trade between the North and South
It linked regions through trade but gave the North and South different interests
It gave the federal government direct control of every farm and factory in the nation
questions.explanation: Canals, railroads, and cotton exports linked Americans, but the Northern and Southern economies developed in different directions.
choiceExplanations: Regions specialized, and the tariff remained controversial.
Trade between the regions grew.
Canals, railroads, and cotton exports linked Americans, but the Northern and Southern economies developed in different directions.
Production stayed in private hands.
questions.distinguisher: The same goods choice is close because markets did unify, but regions specialized in different goods.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in American politics from the 1790s to the 1840s?
choices: Disputes over the role and powers of the federal government continued
The same two parties competed in every election without change
Property requirements for voting were enforced in every state
Congress and the president agreed on the national bank at all times
questions.explanation: Debates about the bank, tariffs, and internal improvements echoed the arguments of Hamilton and Jefferson.
choiceExplanations: Debates about the bank, tariffs, and internal improvements echoed the arguments of Hamilton and Jefferson.
The parties changed from Federalists and Democratic-Republicans to Democrats and Whigs.
Property requirements were dropped in most states.
The bank was a source of conflict.
questions.distinguisher: The same parties choice is close because parties persisted, but their names and makeup changed.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the Louisiana Purchase and the Monroe Doctrine as foreign-policy actions?
choices: The purchase warned European powers away, while the Doctrine added territory to the nation
The purchase added territory, while the Doctrine warned Europe against intervening
The purchase formed an alliance with France, while the Doctrine ended trade with Europe
The purchase ended the war with Britain, while the Doctrine ended the war with Spain
questions.explanation: The purchase of 1803 doubled the nation's size, and the Doctrine of 1823 set a policy toward European powers.
choiceExplanations: The actions are reversed.
The purchase of 1803 doubled the nation's size, and the Doctrine of 1823 set a policy toward European powers.
The purchase was not an alliance, and the Doctrine did not end trade.
Neither action ended a war.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed actions choice is close because it names the same two events, but it assigns the effects to the wrong event.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect of westward expansion on the debate over slavery between 1800 and 1848?
choices: The sections reached a lasting agreement on slavery that ended the debate in Congress
Northerners and Southerners agreed that new territories should be closed to slavery
Congress gave the Western territories the power to decide the question of slavery alone
Disputes such as the Missouri Compromise showed the sections disagreed over slavery in new lands
questions.explanation: Each new addition of land raised the question of the spread of slavery and showed the divisions between the sections.
choiceExplanations: The debate continued.
Southerners opposed closing the territories.
Congress took part in the decisions.
Each new addition of land raised the question of the spread of slavery and showed the divisions between the sections.
questions.distinguisher: The lasting agreement choice is close because the compromise seemed to settle the issue, but it was only temporary.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an effect, rather than a cause, of the Second Great Awakening?
choices: Anxiety about the changes of the market revolution
Democratic and individualistic ideas in the early republic
Increased participation in temperance and antislavery societies
Social and geographical mobility that loosened old ties to churches
questions.explanation: Revivals encouraged believers to join reform societies, which makes reform an effect of the Awakening.
choiceExplanations: That anxiety helped to cause the revivals.
Those ideas were a cause.
Revivals encouraged believers to join reform societies, which makes reform an effect of the Awakening.
Mobility was a cause of the revivals.
questions.distinguisher: The anxiety choice is close because it is linked to the Awakening, but it came before the revivals.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.
